Getting Started with R

Part 1: Intro to the RStudio Interface

Hello, and welcome to this tutorial series on getting started with R. We’re going to start with an introduction to the RStudio interface.

Structure

  • When you first open RStudio, your screen is divided into four sections: the source pane, the console pane, the environment pane, and the output pane.

  • Sometimes, when you first open R, it will look like this, with the console covering the whole left side of the screen:

  • If that is the case, you can bring up the source pane by clicking the two rectangles in the top corner of the console, and that will split the screen between the two of them.

Console (bottom left)

  • The console pane (bottom left) is where the action takes place and where you’ll see most of your output.
  • Right now, the console is showing information about the version of R that I’m using, which is 4.5.2.

  • Here, at the console prompt (blue >), you can run individual lines of code.
    • Let’s start with the classic print("Hello, world!").

  • You run the code by hitting Enter, and your output appears below your code.

  • Here we have some mathematical operations.

  • While in the console, you can use the up and down arrows to to scroll through previous commands in your history.
    • So you can go back to previous code and run it again or edit it quickly without having to type it out again.


Note that while this first tutorial includes lots of screenshots so that you can see what it looks like to type and execute code in the interface, in most cases code will be displayed like this, so it can be copied and pasted:

print("Hello, world!")
## [1] "Hello, world!"

Source pane (top left)

  • The source pane (top left) is basically a notebook, and it’s where you’ll typically do most of your work in R.
  • In the source pane, hitting Enter doesn’t run a line of code, it just adds another line to the script.
    • So you can write multiple lines of code at once, break a long function into multiple lines for easier reading, and write whole scripts.
    • This also makes it easy to return to previous lines of code if you need to edit them or run them again.

  • Returning to some of the commands we ran in the console, we can again print "Hello, world!", do some math, and add a new function called sum(), which adds everything inside together.

  • In the source pane, you run code by having your cursor on the line you want to run, and clicking “Run” at the top right of the pane.
    • The code appears in the console as it runs, and the cursor jumps to the next line.

  • So you can run a series of lines in a row by clicking “Run” over and over, without having to move your mouse.
    • The cursor can be located anywhere on the line (beginning, middle, end).
  • Alternatively, if you want to run a lot of code at once, you can highlight the code and click “Run”.
    • Then down in the console it will print out each line of code and its output separately, but it will do it all at once.

  • One thing you have to note about highlighting is that if you highlight just part of a line (below, just the 29 on line 6), if you click “Run”, you will get the result for just the highlighted part, and not the whole command.

  • There is a keyboard shortcut for running lines of code in the source pane:
    • Windows: Ctrl + Enter; Mac: Command + Enter
    • You can run multiple lines of code quickly by hitting Enter repeatedly while holding the Ctrl/Command key down.
  • Another thing you can do is to leave notes in your code called “comments”.
    • Comments are preceded by #, and when you type them out, the line turns green to show that it is not actual executable code.
    • When R is executing your code, it skips over anything preceded by #.
    • If you click “Run” while your cursor is on a comment, it will run the next line instead.
  • You can leave comments to leave notes for yourself, describing your code, dividing it into sections, or whatever is helpful for you.

  • You can also add comments at the ends of lines of code, and anything on that line that is preceded by # will be left out of the execution.
print("Hello, world!") # first R code!
## [1] "Hello, world!"
  • When you’re happy with the code you’ve written in the source pane, you can save it by going to “File”, “Save” or “Save As”, or using a keyboard shortcut like Ctrl/Command + S.

  • Here I’m going to save to my folder “R Tutorials”, and call this script “tutorial_1”.

  • And now we can see that the title in the top left tab has changed from “Untitled1” to “tutorial_1.R”.

  • If we want to open up any other files, we can do that using “File”, “Open”.
  • To create a new script, click the green plus button in the left corner and choose “R Script”.

  • You can then swap back and forth between the two tabs.

Environment pane (top right)

  • The important parts of the environment pane (top right) are the Environment and History tabs.
  • The Environment tab gives you a list of all the objects that R is currently storing in its memory (so right now, none).

  • We’ll get into objects in the next tutorial, but for now, let’s just create one to show what the environment pane looks like.
  • Let’s create an object called numbers that is just the numbers 1 to 1000, and an object called animals that is a list of animals.
numbers <- 1:1000
animals <- c("dog","cat","fish")
  • When I run these lines of code in the source pane, these objects appear in the environment pane.
  • You can see the type of object they are, their length, and a preview of the content inside.
    • numbers is made of integers and is 1000 long
    • animals is made of characters and is 3 long

  • If you want to see the full content of an object, you can do that by typing its name in the console.

  • So any time you create variables or data frames or functions, they’ll appear in the environment pane with a brief description and/or preview of their content.
  • R will only remember objects created in your current session (so since the last time you opened the software).
  • You can clear the session memory with the broom at the top of the pane, which will “sweep” the environment of all the saved objects.

  • Now if you call numbers in the console, it tells you that the object numbers is not found; it no longer exists.
numbers
## Error:
## ! object 'numbers' not found
  • If we want these objects back, we need to run the code again.
numbers <- 1:1000
animals <- c("dog","cat","fish")

numbers

  • The other important tab is the History tab, which contains a record of all the code that we’ve run during this R session in the order that we ran it.

  • So if you need to find old code that you’ve since edited, or clarify if you ran things in the right order, you can find that out here.

Output pane (bottom right)

  • Finally, we have the output pane in the bottom right.

  • It has three main tabs that you’ll end up using.
    • The most commonly used one is Plots.
      • Whenever you generate a graph or image, it appears here, as I’ll demonstrate in a moment.
    • Another one is the Files tab.
      • Here, it shows the structure of the files and folders on your device.
      • So if I go into “R Tutorials”, you can see that I have an “example_graph.R” script and my current “tutorial_1.R” script.

  • If I save and close tutorial_1.R and then click it in the Files tab, it will open up again so that I can continue to edit or run it.
  • If I open up the example_graph.R code and execute everything in it, the output pane will switch automatically to the Plots tab and show me the graph I have created.

  • You don’t need to understand the example_graph.R code at this stage, but here it is if you’re curious!
library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(
  x = 1:10,
  y = (1:10)^2
)

# Plot with ggplot2
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue", linewidth = 1) + # Line
  geom_point(color = "red", size = 3) +   # Points
  labs(
    title = "Example Graph with ggplot2",
    x = "X Values",
    y = "Y Values (X squared)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

  • Last we have the Help tab, which is where you can look up the documentation for functions and find out how to use them.

  • If we look up the function sum() that we used earlier, we can see that it has a description, it tells what it does, it tells the arguments that it uses, and it gives a lengthy set of details about how it is used

  • All of this can be really overwhelming at first. But what’s really helpful is if you scroll all the way down to the bottom, you get a list of examples of how to use the function.
    • You can run those to see what they do, or use them as a reference to construct your own code.

  • So this is what RStudio looks like. And with that, we’re ready to begin looking at some coding basics in Part 2.
